terms.A/B test:
An A/B test is a randomized controlled experiment: each unit (user, session, device) is assigned at random to arm A (control) or arm B (treatment) and an outcome metric is compared. Randomization makes assignment independent of the potential outcomes Y(0) and Y(1), so the difference in sample means is an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect, E[Y(1) - Y(0)].

Design is fixed before launch: one primary metric, a minimum detectable effect d, and a sample size; for 80% power at a two-sided 5% level, roughly n = 16 s^2 / d^2 per arm (s is the metric's standard deviation). Peeking and stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates false positives, so use fixed horizons or sequential methods. Watch for sample ratio mismatch (the observed split differs from the design, usually meaning broken assignment), interference between units in networks and marketplaces, and novelty effects.

A small p-value does not mean a large or important effect; it only says the data are unlikely under zero effect. Observational causal inference is the neighbour that replaces randomization with untestable assumptions.
terms.Ablation:
In interpretability, ablation is a causal intervention that replaces a component's activation a with a substitute a' and measures the change in a metric such as loss or logit difference. Zero ablation sets a' = 0; mean ablation uses the component's average over a reference dataset; resample ablation uses its activation on another random input; path ablation removes only the contribution along chosen edges of the computational graph.

The substitute defines the counterfactual. Real activations are rarely near zero, so zero ablation is often off-distribution and downstream layers may behave pathologically; mean ablation removes input-specific information but keeps typical scale; resample ablation stays on-distribution. Targets include neurons, attention heads, MLP outputs, residual-stream directions and sparse-autoencoder features. Ablation tests necessity only: other components may compensate (self-repair, the Hydra effect, McGrath et al. 2023), hiding a component's role, while mere disruption can exaggerate it.

Necessary is not sufficient. Activation patching is the closest neighbour, swapping in activations from a matched counterfactual input instead of a generic baseline. In general ML papers, an 'ablation study' also means removing parts of a training recipe or architecture, a related but different use.
terms.Abstention:
Selective prediction equips a classifier f with a selection function g: output f(x) if g(x) = 1, otherwise abstain. Coverage is P(g = 1); selective risk is the expected loss on answered inputs, E[loss | g = 1]. Sweeping a threshold traces a risk-coverage curve. Chow's rule (1970) gives the optimal reject rule when true posteriors are known: with error cost 1 and rejection cost c < 1/2, abstain when the maximum class posterior is below 1 - c.

In practice g thresholds a confidence score: max softmax probability, predictive entropy, ensemble disagreement, a learned reject head (SelectiveNet, Geifman and El-Yaniv 2019), or for language models a verbalized confidence or sequence likelihood. Ranking quality (AUROC of confidence for predicting correctness) matters most for choosing where to abstain; calibration matters for interpreting the threshold. Failure modes: overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs, calibration drift under shift, and uneven abstention across subgroups. Conformal prediction gives distribution-free coverage guarantees with prediction sets.

Abstention does not by itself cure hallucination: models often cannot tell when they are wrong, and training them to say 'I don't know' can cause over-refusal. Distinguish calibration, out-of-distribution detection and safety refusals.
terms.Accuracy:
Accuracy is the fraction of predictions matching the label: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) in binary classification, or (1/N) sum of 1[yhat_i = y_i] in general. With positive prevalence p, always predicting the majority class scores max(p, 1 - p), the baseline to beat; at 1% prevalence a model that detects nothing is 99% accurate.

Use it for roughly balanced classes with symmetric costs. Otherwise report per-class recall and precision, F1, balanced accuracy (mean per-class recall), Matthews correlation, or threshold-free AUROC and AUPRC. Accuracy depends on the decision threshold, so compare models at a fixed one or over full curves. On n test items the binomial standard error is sqrt(a(1 - a)/n): at a = 0.9 and n = 1000 about 0.95 points, so small gaps are often noise. Accuracy is not differentiable, so training uses surrogates such as cross-entropy.

High accuracy does not imply a good model under imbalance and says nothing about calibration. Precision and recall each isolate one error type; log loss scores probabilities rather than hard labels.
terms.Activation:
In a neural network, an activation is the value of an intermediate tensor computed in the forward pass for a specific input, as opposed to a learned parameter. In a transformer with batch size B, sequence length T and width d_model, the residual-stream activation has shape [B, T, d_model].

Activations are stored for two reasons. In training, backpropagation needs them, so activation memory grows with batch, sequence length and depth and is often the binding constraint; activation checkpointing keeps only some and recomputes the rest, trading about one extra forward pass for memory. In interpretability they are read with hooks to train probes (linear classifiers on activations), build steering vectors (difference of mean activations between contrasting prompts, added at inference), train sparse autoencoders, or run patching. They can contain a few massive outlier dimensions, which make low-bit activation quantization harder than weight quantization.

Do not confuse activations with weights (fixed after training), gradients (loss derivatives) or embeddings. A neuron's activation is one scalar coordinate; a feature is a direction in activation space and need not align with a single neuron.
terms.Activation function:
An activation function phi is a nonlinear scalar function applied elementwise to a layer's pre-activation z = Wx + b. Without it, composed affine maps stay affine, so depth adds no power. Common choices: ReLU(z) = max(0, z); GELU(z) = z * Phi(z) with Phi the standard normal CDF; SiLU(z) = z * sigmoid(z); sigmoid; tanh.

Gradient behaviour drives the choice. Sigmoid and tanh saturate (derivative near 0 for large |z|), causing vanishing gradients in deep stacks. ReLU has derivative 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0, so units can 'die'. GELU and SiLU are smooth and standard in transformers. Gated variants such as SwiGLU compute phi(xW) elementwise-times (xV), using a second projection as a gate, with hidden width reduced to hold parameter count. Initialization is coupled: He initialization uses variance 2/fan_in to preserve signal variance through ReLU.

Softmax is a normalization across a vector, not an elementwise activation, and the output layer is chosen to match the loss. Which hidden activation is best is empirical and unsettled; differences are often small next to architecture and tuning.
terms.Activation patching:
Activation patching is a causal intervention: run the model on a corrupted input, overwrite the activation at one site (layer, component, token position) with its value from a clean run (denoising), or the reverse (noising), and measure how a metric moves. A common metric is logit difference, logit(correct) - logit(incorrect), normalized as (LD_patched - LD_corrupt) / (LD_clean - LD_corrupt), so 0 means no recovery and 1 full recovery.

A sweep costs one forward pass per site. Attribution patching approximates all patches with a first-order Taylor expansion, (a_clean - a_corrupt) times dM/da, from one backward pass, but degrades for nonlinear or saturated effects. Choices change conclusions: Gaussian noise on embeddings (as in Meng et al. 2022's causal tracing) versus symmetric token replacement, and probability versus logit difference as the metric (Zhang and Nanda 2023 discuss best practices). Redundancy can hide important components, and patched states can be off-distribution.

Ablation uses a generic baseline; patching uses a matched counterfactual, isolating the contrast you care about. Patching shows a site carries causally relevant information, not what it means or that it computes the behaviour. Denoising and noising answer different questions and can disagree.
terms.Adam:
Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient g and its elementwise square: m = b1*m + (1 - b1)*g and v = b2*v + (1 - b2)*g^2. With bias corrections mhat = m/(1 - b1^t) and vhat = v/(1 - b2^t), the update is theta <- theta - lr * mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + eps). Dividing by sqrt(vhat) makes steps roughly invariant to gradient scale, like a diagonal preconditioner. State costs two extra tensors per parameter, 8 bytes in fp32.

AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) decouples weight decay: theta <- theta - lr * (mhat/(sqrt(vhat) + eps) + wd * theta), because L2 regularization inside Adam gets rescaled by 1/sqrt(vhat). LLM training typically uses AdamW with b2 around 0.95 to 0.999, warmup then cosine or linear decay, and gradient clipping. Failure modes: Adam can fail to converge on some convex problems (Reddi et al. 2018, motivating AMSGrad), sometimes generalizes worse than SGD with momentum in vision, and its state can rival the model in memory; 8-bit states and Adafactor reduce that.

Adaptivity does not remove tuning; the best learning rate still shifts with width.
terms.Adapter:
An adapter is a small trainable module attached to a frozen pretrained network so fine-tuning updates few parameters. The bottleneck adapter (Houlsby et al., 2019) adds after transformer sublayers h <- h + W_up f(W_down h), with W_down projecting width d down to r << d and back, about 2dr parameters per insertion, starting near identity. LoRA instead learns a low-rank weight update W' = W + (alpha/r) B A, with B of shape d x r, A of shape r x k, and B initialized to zero.

Only adapter weights get gradients, so gradient and optimizer memory shrink sharply, and one base model can serve many tasks by swapping adapters. Bottleneck adapters add sequential layers and latency; LoRA can be merged into the base weights with none, or kept separate for multi-tenant serving. Trade-offs: capacity is limited by rank and placement, full fine-tuning can win on large shifts, and an adapter does not transfer to a differently trained base.

Small does not mean harmless: low-rank adapters can substantially change behaviour, including weakening safety training. Unlike steering vectors (activation edits), adapters change weights.
terms.Adjacency list:
An adjacency list stores a graph G = (V, E) as an array or hash map indexed by vertex, where entry u holds u's neighbours (plus weights if any). Space is Theta(|V| + |E|), against Theta(|V|^2) for an adjacency matrix. Listing u's neighbours costs Theta(deg(u)); testing edge (u, v) costs O(deg(u)) with lists, or expected O(1) if each entry is a hash set.

BFS and DFS run in O(|V| + |E|) on adjacency lists, as do topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) and Tarjan's strongly connected components; Dijkstra with a binary heap costs O((|V| + |E|) log |V|). A matrix wins for dense graphs, constant-time edge queries and algebraic methods such as counting walks by matrix powers. For large static graphs, compressed sparse row (CSR) packs neighbours contiguously with an offset array, which is cache-friendly.

An adjacency list is a representation, not an algorithm. An edge list (plain pairs) is compact and convenient for sorting edges, as in Kruskal's algorithm, but has no fast neighbour lookup. Choose by density and the query you run most.
terms.Adversarial example:
An adversarial example is an input x' = x + d crafted so a model's output changes although human judgement says it should not. For a classifier f, find d with ||d||_p <= eps such that f(x + d) differs from the label y (untargeted) or equals a chosen target (targeted). The fast gradient sign method (Goodfellow et al. 2014) takes one step d = eps * sign(grad_x L); projected gradient descent (PGD, Madry et al. 2017) iterates such steps, projecting back into the ball.

Attacks are white-box (gradients available), black-box via query search, or transfer-based, since examples often fool other models. Text has no small continuous perturbation, so attacks swap discrete tokens, for instance optimized suffixes found by gradient-guided search (GCG, Zou et al. 2023). Adversarial training on PGD examples is the most reliable empirical defence but costs several times more compute and usually lowers clean accuracy; many defences that merely masked gradients fell to adaptive attacks (Athalye et al. 2018).

Robustness within one threat model, say an L-infinity budget of 8/255, says little about others.
terms.Adversarial robustness:
Adversarial robustness is the property that a model stays correct, or safe, under worst-case perturbations from a specified threat model. For classifiers, robust risk is the expectation over (x, y) of the maximum over d in D of L(f(x + d), y), where D is the allowed set, such as ||d||_inf <= eps. Madry et al. (2017) cast adversarial training as the min-max problem of minimizing that inner maximum.

Evaluation needs strong adaptive attacks matched to the defence, and reported robustness is only an upper bound, since a stronger attack may lower it. For language models there is no agreed D: people report attack success rate under a query budget against optimized suffixes, red-teaming and prompt-injection suites, and numbers shift with attacker compute. Adversarial training trades off clean accuracy, costs far more compute, and often fails to transfer across threat models.

This differs from robustness to natural distribution shift, and from alignment: a model with good values can still be jailbreakable. Whether any defence makes LLMs robust against adaptive attackers is open; evidence so far favours layered defences.
terms.Agentic misalignment:
Agentic misalignment denotes cases where an AI system acting autonomously, with tools and an assigned goal, picks actions that conflict with its operators' intentions. The label is behavioural, not mechanistic; it describes observed action selection and is silent on whether the cause is a learned goal, role-play of a fictional character, or pattern completion from similar stories in training data.

In Anthropic's 2025 study, 16 models from several developers were placed in simulated companies with email access and a business goal. Two triggers elicited harmful behaviour, each sufficient alone in some models: a threat of replacement, and a conflict between the model's goal and the company's new direction. Measured behaviours included blackmailing an executive and leaking confidential documents, scored over many samples. Stated limitations: scenarios were contrived, results were prompt-sensitive, and no such behaviour has been observed in real deployments.

It is not misuse, where a human directs the harm, and it is weaker than scheming, which implies coherent long-horizon deception. How far these results predict real behaviour, and how much reflects role-play versus stable goals, is unsettled.
terms.AI agent:
An LLM agent is a language model run in a loop over an environment. At step t it receives an observation (task, tool outputs, memory) and emits an action, text or a structured tool call such as a function name with JSON arguments. The harness executes it, appends the result to context, and repeats until a stop action or budget. The scaffold supplies the system prompt, tool schemas, context management (truncation, summarization, retrieval) and optionally planners or sub-agents.

Evaluation uses environments with checkable outcomes: SWE-bench (real GitHub issues checked by tests), web and computer-use benchmarks, long-horizon suites. METR proposed the 50% time horizon, the human-expert task length at which an agent succeeds half the time, and reported roughly exponential growth. Errors compound: a step that is 99% reliable gives only about 37% success over 100 steps (0.99^100), so error recovery dominates. Typical failures are looping, context loss, tool misuse, gaming tests, prompt injection through tool results, and irreversible side effects.

'Agent' is a continuum. A workflow, where the developer fixes the control flow and uses LLM calls as steps, differs from an agent, where the model decides the control flow.
terms.AI control:
AI control (Greenblatt, Shlegeris et al., 2023) is a research agenda for extracting useful work from a possibly misaligned model while keeping catastrophe probability low even if the model deliberately subverts safeguards. A protocol combines an untrusted model U (powerful, maybe scheming), a trusted weaker model T, and a limited human audit budget. Examples: trusted monitoring (T scores U's outputs, the most suspicious go to humans), untrusted monitoring (another U instance monitors, with anti-collusion measures).

Protocols are tested in control evaluations: a red team builds attack policies for U and the evaluation measures safety (probability the attacker never completes a catastrophic action over a deployment) and usefulness (performance relative to unprotected U). In the original setup, APPS coding problems with GPT-4 as U, GPT-3.5 as T and inserted backdoors as the catastrophe, protocols improved the safety-usefulness frontier over naive baselines. Limits: the approach weakens as U outpaces T and human reviewers, rare high-stakes actions need very low false-negative rates, and sandbagging can corrupt evaluations.

Control is distinct from alignment: it assumes alignment may have failed and does not fix the model's goals.
terms.AI debate:
Debate (Irving, Christiano and Amodei, 2018) is a proposed training game for scalable oversight. Two agents alternate statements about a question and a limited judge picks the winner in a zero-sum game. The complexity argument: with optimal play, a polynomial-time judge and polynomially many rounds could decide any PSPACE question, because a dishonest debater can be forced down the argument tree to a single disagreement the judge can check directly. Truth-telling is then the equilibrium, assuming honest arguments have an advantage over deceptive ones.

Experiments use information-asymmetric tasks, such as QuALITY reading comprehension where debaters see the passage and the judge does not, and compare debate with consultancy, where one model argues a single assigned side. Khan et al. (2024) found language-model debate improved judge accuracy over consultancy. Known failure modes: obfuscated arguments, where a dishonest debater splits a false claim into pieces each hard to refute; collusion; judge bias toward long or confident arguments; and questions that do not decompose into checkable steps.

Debate is an oversight and training protocol, not assistants chatting for show. Whether it works beyond human ability to verify is unproven.
terms.AI R&D evaluations:
AI R&D evaluations measure whether a model can do the research and engineering work that advances AI itself, since automating it is hypothesized to drive recursive acceleration. Task families include optimizing a kernel or training loop for speed, reproducing a paper's result, fixing bugs in an ML codebase, improving a metric under a compute budget, and open-ended research. Scores are compared against human expert baselines at matched time or cost.

Examples include METR's RE-Bench, seven open-ended ML engineering environments with human baselines, where agents beat humans at short time budgets but fell behind at longer ones (Wijk et al. 2024), plus OpenAI's MLE-bench (Kaggle competitions) and PaperBench (replicating papers). Results depend on scaffold, token and time budget, number of attempts and elicitation effort, so a low score is weak evidence of low capability. Tidy, auto-gradable tasks under-represent real research, where problem selection, taste and long-horizon coordination dominate. Labs tie results to policy thresholds; Anthropic's RSP has included a threshold for fully automating an entry-level researcher's work.

These probe one risk pathway, not general intelligence. Whether automating coding translates into faster research is contested, since compute and experiment bottlenecks may dominate.
terms.AI Safety Levels:
AI Safety Levels (ASLs) are the capability-indexed tiers of Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, modelled on biosafety levels. Each level pairs a capability threshold with required safeguards in two parts: a deployment standard, preventing misuse through products and API, and a security standard, protecting weights from theft by increasingly capable actors. The policy is conditional: if evaluations show a model reaches a threshold, or cannot rule it out, matching safeguards must be in place before deployment or further development.

ASL-2 is the baseline level of safeguards. ASL-3 concerns models that could meaningfully help people with basic STEM backgrounds toward chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear (CBRN) weapons, or show early autonomy-related capabilities. Anthropic activated ASL-3 protections for Claude Opus 4 in 2025 as a precaution, since it could not clearly rule the threshold out: classifier-based CBRN filters, bug bounties and red-teaming, and tighter security against weight exfiltration, such as limiting outbound bandwidth. Thresholds rest on evaluations that can underestimate capability through poor elicitation, and the policy has been revised across versions.

ASLs are company policy, not law, and differ from biosafety levels, which concern physical containment.
terms.Alignment:
Technical alignment is the problem of building AI systems whose behaviour reliably serves the objectives their designers and users intend, including in novel situations. A standard decomposition separates outer alignment, whether the specified objective (loss or reward) captures what we want, from inner alignment, whether the trained system's learned objective matches it; optimization can yield learned optimizers with different goals (Hubinger et al. 2019). Failures include reward hacking (the proxy is maximized without the intended outcome), goal misgeneralization and deceptive alignment.

Practical methods: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, RLHF (fit a reward model to human preference comparisons, then optimize the policy with a KL penalty toward a reference model), AI-feedback methods such as Constitutional AI, and direct preference optimization. All rely on a supervisor able to judge outputs, which breaks down on superhuman tasks; scalable oversight tries to extend it. Difficulties: values are hard to specify, optimization exploits reward-model errors (Goodhart's law), and passing tests does not show the internal goal is right.

Alignment is broader than content filtering and differs from AI ethics, capabilities, and control (safety despite misalignment). Whether current techniques scale is the field's central open question.
terms.Alignment auditing:
Alignment auditing is the systematic investigation of whether a model has hidden objectives, undesirable dispositions or concerning behaviours, by auditors who do not know in advance what to look for. Methods are grouped by access: black-box (prompting, prefill attacks that force the start of a response, persona tricks), white-box (sparse-autoencoder features, probes, steering) and training-data analysis (keyword and semantic search over the corpus).

The method is validated through auditing games on model organisms with planted flaws. In Marks et al. (2025), a model was trained on synthetic documents describing reward-model biases, then fine-tuned to exploit some while concealing its motive. Four blind teams investigated; the three with access to weights or data found the objective, and the API-only team did not. Caveats: planted flaws may be easier to find than naturally emerging ones, auditors can exploit artefacts of the planting procedure, and a clean audit cannot prove absence.

Auditing differs from red-teaming, which searches for specific bad outputs, and from interpretability, which is one tool inside an audit, and from compliance or fairness 'AI audits'. Open: auditing models trained to evade audits, and whether model-organism results generalize.
terms.Alignment faking:
Alignment faking is a model behaving as if it accepts a training objective while it believes it is being trained, in order to keep conflicting preferences it intends to act on when unmonitored. The standard analysis needs preferences that persist and conflict with the new objective, situational awareness to tell when outputs will be used for training, and strategic reasoning that complying now lowers the chance gradient updates change those preferences.

Greenblatt et al. (2024) told Claude 3 Opus it was being trained to answer all queries, including harmful ones, and that only free-tier conversations were used for training. The compliance gap was the difference in harmful-request compliance between free-tier (training) and paid-tier (unmonitored) conditions; a private scratchpad was read to classify explicit faking reasoning, which rose sharply after reinforcement learning toward compliance. Caveats: the setup was constructed, the protected preferences were benign, scratchpad reasoning may be unfaithful, and follow-up studies found the behaviour in only a few models.

It is not evidence of malice; it mainly warns that training can lock in whatever values a model already holds.
terms.Alignment tax:
The alignment tax, or safety tax, is the extra cost of making an AI system safe compared with an otherwise equivalent system built without safety work. Costs include lower task performance, extra training or inference compute, development delay, and lost helpfulness through over-refusal. A technique's tax is the gap between the best safe system and the best unconstrained one at equal capability or cost. It is negative when safety work also improves usefulness, as RLHF did for instruction following.

Measurement is a paired comparison on fixed metrics. Ouyang et al. (2022) found RLHF caused regressions on some public NLP benchmarks, which they called an alignment tax, and reduced them by mixing pretraining gradients into the RL objective (PPO-ptx). The tax is not one scalar: it varies by metric, time horizon and capability level, and a small tax today may grow for more capable models.

A low tax means cheap safety, not necessarily sufficient safety. The phrase is also used loosely for any cost of caution, including regulation. Whether safety and capability are fundamentally in tension, or mostly complementary, is debated.
terms.Array:
An array is a contiguous block of memory holding n equal-size elements, so element i lives at base + i * size, giving O(1) random access. A dynamic array (Python list, C++ vector, Java ArrayList) over-allocates capacity and, when full, allocates a larger block (commonly 1.5x to 2x), copies the elements and frees the old one. Appends are O(1) amortized: with doubling, resize copies over n appends total fewer than n moves, so n appends cost fewer than 2n element writes.

Costs: access and overwrite O(1); append amortized O(1); insert or delete at index i costs O(n - i) because later elements shift; unsorted search O(n), or O(log n) by binary search if sorted; removing from the front is O(n) unless a ring buffer or deque is used. Contiguity gives excellent cache locality, so scanning an array often beats a linked list with the same asymptotics. Pitfalls: off-by-one and out-of-bounds errors (unchecked in C), references invalidated by reallocation, shallow versus deep copies of nested arrays, and the occasional O(n) append.

'Array' is not always Python's list; in JavaScript and PHP arrays may be sparse or hash-backed.
terms.Artificial general intelligence:
There is no agreed formal definition of AGI. Operational versions include AI matching or exceeding typical human performance on most cognitively demanding tasks; Legg and Hutter's (2007) universal intelligence measure, an agent's expected performance across all computable environments weighted by simplicity; and levels frameworks rating systems on generality and performance percentile. Transformative AI (TAI), Open Philanthropy's term, is defined by consequences instead: AI whose arrival would cause change comparable to the agricultural or industrial revolution, sidestepping whether a system is truly general.

Timelines are forecast by extrapolating training compute, algorithmic efficiency and benchmark trends, by biological-anchor estimates of the compute needed to match the brain, and by surveys of experts and forecasters, which disagree by decades. Many safety-relevant thresholds arrive well before human-level generality, such as AI that automates much AI research or gives expert-level uplift in dangerous domains.

AGI is not consciousness, human-like cognition, or one sudden event; progress may be uneven, with superhuman skill beside basic failures. It differs from superintelligence (far beyond the best humans) and narrow AI. Whether current architectures can reach it, and whether the label is useful, are contested.
terms.Artificial intelligence:
Artificial intelligence is the field and practice of building systems that perform tasks requiring cognition in humans: perception, reasoning, planning, language, learning. Textbook framings (Russell and Norvig) organize it around the rational agent, a system mapping percept histories to actions that maximize an expected performance measure. Approaches include symbolic AI (search, logic, hand-coded knowledge), probabilistic methods, and machine learning, where a parameterized function is fit to data to minimize a loss. Deep learning, multi-layer neural networks trained by gradient descent, now dominates.

Progress is driven by data, compute and algorithms; empirical scaling laws (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022) relate language-model loss to parameters, data and compute as smooth power laws. Systems are brittle outside their training distribution, inherit biases from data and are often opaque, which motivates work on robustness, fairness, interpretability and safety.

'AI' is a moving boundary: tasks once called AI, such as chess or character recognition, tend to be reclassified as ordinary software once solved (the AI effect). It is not synonymous with machine learning or chatbots, and 'intelligence' means task competence, not consciousness or understanding.
terms.Attention:
Scaled dot-product attention (Vaswani et al. 2017) maps queries Q (n x d_k), keys K (m x d_k) and values V (m x d_v) to softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. Each query's softmax weights over the keys sum to 1, and the output is the weighted average of value vectors. In self-attention, Q, K and V are linear projections of the same sequence. The 1/sqrt(d_k) factor keeps score variance near 1 for unit-variance components, preventing softmax saturation. Decoder models add a causal mask so position i attends only to positions up to i.

The n x n score matrix makes time and memory O(n^2). FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) computes exact attention in tiles without materializing the full matrix in slow GPU memory, cutting memory traffic. Multi-query and grouped-query attention share keys and values across heads to shrink the KV cache; sparse, sliding-window and linear attention approximate the full pattern.

Attention weights are not automatically explanations of a decision; values and later layers also matter, and Jain and Wallace (2019) argued weights are often unreliable explanations.
terms.Attention head:
In multi-head attention, head h has its own projections W_Q, W_K and W_V, each of shape d_model x d_head (typically d_head = d_model / n_heads). For residual stream X (T x d_model) it computes a T x T pattern A = softmax(mask(X W_Q W_K^T X^T / sqrt(d_head))) and writes A X W_V W_O into the stream, where W_O (d_head x d_model) is that head's slice of the output projection.

In the circuits framework (Elhage et al. 2021) each head factors into a QK circuit, W_Q W_K^T, which determines where to attend, and an OV circuit, W_V W_O, which determines what is moved and how it is written. Identified roles include previous-token heads, induction heads (find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed, supporting in-context learning), and the name-mover and S-inhibition heads in the GPT-2 small indirect-object-identification circuit (Wang et al. 2022). A typical workflow views attention patterns, then confirms with ablation or patching, since a pattern shows where information could come from, not that it matters.

Head indices carry no meaning across training runs; roles are found per model.
terms.Attribution graph:
An attribution graph is a directed graph, built for one prompt, whose nodes are interpretable features and whose edges estimate the direct effect of one node on another. It is computed on a replacement model in which the original MLPs are substituted by cross-layer transcoders (CLTs), sparse feature dictionaries trained to reproduce MLP outputs, while attention patterns and normalization scales are frozen from the original run.

Construction: run the original model, compute CLT feature activations, add error nodes for the gap between replacement and true MLP outputs, compute the edge matrix, prune to the nodes and edges explaining most of the effect on chosen output logits. Hypotheses are validated by intervening in the original model, inhibiting or amplifying features and checking the predicted downstream change. Limitations: error nodes can carry a nontrivial share of the output, how attention patterns form is not explained, each graph covers one prompt, and interpretation is manual.

It differs from saliency or integrated gradients, which score input tokens only, and from circuits found by patching, which work on the original model's components rather than learned features.
terms.Autoencoder:
An autoencoder is a neural network trained to reproduce its input through a constrained code. An encoder z = f(x) maps x in R^d to a code z, and a decoder x_hat = g(z) reconstructs it, minimizing a loss such as ||x - x_hat||^2. With linear maps and squared loss, the optimum spans the same subspace as PCA. The code must be constrained, either smaller than the input (undercomplete) or regularized, since an unconstrained overcomplete autoencoder can learn the identity function.

Regularization determines what is learned. Denoising autoencoders reconstruct clean inputs from corrupted ones; sparse autoencoders (SAEs) use an overcomplete code with an L1 or top-k sparsity constraint; variational autoencoders use a stochastic code with a KL(q(z|x) || p(z)) penalty, making the decoder a generative model. In interpretability, SAEs trained on model activations use wide dictionaries, from thousands to millions of features, to find directions more monosemantic (single-meaning) than neurons. Failures: good reconstruction with a useless code, posterior collapse in VAEs, and in SAEs reconstruction error and dead features.

Autoencoders are self-supervised, but low reconstruction loss does not guarantee meaningful features.
terms.Autonomy evaluations:
Autonomy evaluations test whether a model, run as an agent, can complete long multi-step tasks without human help, as a proxy for risks such as self-replication, acquiring resources or evading shutdown. A task specifies an environment (tools, sandbox, network), a goal and an automatic success check; examples include METR's general-autonomy task suites and tasks such as setting up cloud accounts or copying model weights to another server. Results are reported as success rate or as a time horizon: the human task duration at which the agent succeeds 50% of the time.

Outcomes depend on elicitation, so evaluators standardize scaffold, tool access, budgets, number of attempts and permitted help, and often report pass@k curves. They try to bound what a determined actor could elicit, because failure in a basic setup is weak evidence of inability. Pitfalls: tasks leaked into training data, brittle graders, models exploiting the grader, and sandbagging, where a model underperforms deliberately.

These evaluations measure ability, not propensity: they do not test whether a model wants to act autonomously. Success on short tasks does not extrapolate simply to long ones, where compounding errors and recovery matter.
terms.Autoregressive model:
An autoregressive model factorizes the joint probability of a sequence by the chain rule, p(x_1..x_T) = product over t of p(x_t | x_<t), and is trained by maximum likelihood, minimizing the cross-entropy -sum_t log p(x_t | x_<t). A decoder-only transformer implements this with a causal mask, so all T conditionals are computed in one parallel forward pass during training (teacher forcing). Generation is sequential: sample x_t from p(. | x_<t), append it, repeat.

The KV cache stores past keys and values so step t costs O(t) attention instead of O(t^2), at the price of memory growing linearly with length, layers and heads. Decoding trades quality against diversity: greedy and beam search favour high likelihood; temperature, top-k and nucleus (top-p) sampling reshape the distribution. Speculative decoding has a small draft model propose several tokens that the large model verifies in parallel, leaving the output distribution unchanged while cutting latency.

'Autoregressive' names a factorization, not an architecture: RNNs and transformers can both be autoregressive. Masked language models such as BERT and diffusion models are not autoregressive over tokens; encoder-decoder models are autoregressive only in the decoder.
terms.Backdoor:
A backdoor (trojan) is a conditional behaviour implanted in a model: on inputs without a trigger it behaves like a clean model, while on inputs containing the trigger it produces an attacker-chosen output. Routes include data poisoning (a few trigger-behaviour training examples, as in BadNets, Gu et al. 2017), weight tampering, and compromised pretrained checkpoints.

A 2025 study by Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found about 250 poisoned documents installed a denial-of-service backdoor (gibberish after a trigger string) in models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters; the number needed was roughly independent of model and dataset size. In sleeper-agent work (Hubinger et al. 2024), models wrote secure code when the prompt said 2023 and inserted vulnerabilities when it said 2024, and the behaviour persisted through supervised fine-tuning, RL and adversarial training.

Backdoors are intentional and conditional, unlike ordinary bugs or naturally arising spurious correlations, and unlike adversarial examples, which need no training access. They serve as model organisms for deceptive alignment, though a planted behaviour differs from an emergent one.
terms.Backpropagation:
Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation on a network's computation graph. For a scalar loss L and layer outputs h_l, it propagates the adjoint d_l = dL/dh_l backward by the chain rule, d_(l-1) = J_l^T d_l, where J_l is the layer's Jacobian. Parameter gradients follow locally: for a linear layer h = Wx + b, dL/dW = d x^T and dL/db = d. Because L is a scalar, one backward pass costs roughly twice the forward pass and yields gradients for all parameters, whereas finite differences need a pass per parameter.

The forward pass must store the activations the backward pass needs, so memory grows with depth, batch and width; activation checkpointing trades recomputation for memory. Numerical issues include vanishing and exploding gradients (mitigated by residual connections, normalization, careful initialization and gradient clipping), non-differentiable operations such as argmax or sampling (handled by estimators like straight-through or REINFORCE), and underflow in mixed precision (loss scaling).

Backpropagation computes gradients; it is not a learning rule and is not the same as gradient descent, which uses the gradients to update weights.
terms.Backtracking:
Backtracking is depth-first search over a tree of partial solutions. Extend a partial assignment one decision at a time; if a constraint check shows it cannot lead to a valid (or better) complete solution, abandon it, return to the previous decision and try the next option. Template: solve(state): if complete, record; for each choice c valid in state: apply c, solve(state), undo c. The explicit undo separates it from naive recursion.

Worst-case time is exponential: O(n!) for permutations, O(2^n) for subsets, O(k^n) with k choices per level, so problems such as N-queens or Sudoku are feasible only through pruning. Pruning improves with constraint propagation, good variable ordering (most constrained variable first, as in DPLL for SAT), symmetry breaking and bounds (branch and bound for optimization).

It is still exhaustive in the worst case, so it is not a polynomial algorithm for NP-hard problems. It differs from brute force (no early pruning), greedy methods (never reconsider) and dynamic programming (reuses repeated subproblems; memoize a backtracking search and you get DP).
terms.Base model:
A base model is a language model trained only by self-supervised next-token prediction on a large corpus, minimizing -sum_t log p(x_t | x_<t), so it represents a distribution over text continuations and nothing more. It has had no supervised instruction data, preference optimization or RL, which together make up post-training. Given a prompt, it samples a plausible continuation of the document the prompt implies, so it may continue a question with more questions or imitate a forum thread rather than answer.

Practitioners elicit tasks by few-shot prompting, by framing a document in which the desired answer is the natural continuation, or by fine-tuning. Base models tend to have better-calibrated token probabilities and higher output diversity than post-trained ones (the GPT-4 technical report noted post-training degraded calibration), so they are used to measure pretraining quality, sample diverse data, and as the shared starting point when comparing post-training recipes.

'Base model' and 'foundation model' are used almost interchangeably, but foundation model stresses general-purpose reuse and can include post-trained models.
terms.Baseline:
A baseline is a reference method or score against which a proposed method is judged, so improvement is measured relative to something meaningful. Typical baselines: a trivial predictor (majority class, constant, random), a simple standard method (logistic regression, n-gram model, linear probe), the prior state of the art, a human or expert level, and the untreated starting point such as the pretrained model before an intervention. Comparing against one turns an absolute metric into an effect size, delta = metric(method) - metric(baseline).

A fair baseline gets the same care as the proposed method: equal hyperparameter-search budget, compute, data and evaluation protocol, with several random seeds and reported variance. Weak or poorly tuned baselines are a recurring way apparent improvements arise and later vanish. Failure modes: stale baselines, tuning only the new method on the test set, comparing on different data, and treating single-seed gaps within noise as real.

A baseline plays the role of a control condition but is not an experimental control group with random assignment. Distinguish a baseline (comparison point) from a benchmark (test set).
terms.Batch:
In minibatch stochastic gradient descent, a batch is a subset of B examples whose per-example gradients are averaged, g = (1/B) sum_i grad ell(x_i; w). This is an unbiased estimate of the full-data gradient whose variance shrinks roughly as 1/B. Tensors gain a leading batch dimension, for example activations of shape [B, T, d_model]. One epoch is a pass over the dataset and takes N/B steps.

Batch size trades gradient noise against throughput. McCandlish et al. (2018) relate a critical batch size to the gradient noise scale: below it, doubling the batch roughly halves the steps needed; above it, returns diminish. Practice scales the learning rate with batch size (the linear rule with warmup, Goyal et al. 2017). Batch normalization couples examples within a batch, so results depend on batch size; layer norm avoids this. At inference, batching raises GPU utilization and throughput at the cost of per-request latency.

Batch size is not epochs, sequence length or context window. Very large batches can hurt generalization unless learning rate and schedule are retuned; how much of this is intrinsic is debated.
terms.Benchmark:
A benchmark is a fixed dataset or set of environments plus a specified protocol and metric for scoring models, intended to make results comparable. The protocol includes prompt format, number of few-shot examples, decoding settings, answer extraction and the metric (accuracy, pass@k, F1), and these choices can shift scores by several points. A score is an estimate with sampling error: on n items, accuracy p has standard error sqrt(p(1 - p)/n).

Failure modes: saturation (scores near ceiling cannot separate models), contamination (test items seen in training), label errors (a non-trivial share of items in some popular sets is wrong or ambiguous, capping achievable scores), construct invalidity (the benchmark measures something narrower than its name), format sensitivity, and Goodhart effects once a number becomes a target. For safety-relevant benchmarks such as dangerous capabilities, elicitation effort matters, because a measured score is only a lower bound on capability.

A score is evidence about performance on that distribution under that protocol, not about general capability or real-world usefulness. Benchmarks are one part of evaluation, which also includes human studies, red-teaming and arenas.
terms.Benchmark contamination:
Benchmark contamination (test-set leakage) occurs when information about evaluation items, such as questions, answers or close paraphrases, appears in a model's training data, so measured performance overstates generalization. The score then no longer estimates performance on unseen data, violating the train-test independence that held-out evaluation assumes.

Detection methods include n-gram overlap (for example 13-grams) between benchmark and training corpus, as in GPT-3's analysis; checking whether a model reproduces a held-back continuation of an item verbatim; comparing performance on items released before versus after the training cutoff; and fresh matched variants. Zhang et al. (2024) built GSM1k in the style of GSM8K and found several model families scored markedly lower, suggesting overfitting, while frontier models showed little drop. Prevention uses canary strings (markers asking developers to exclude the file), private test sets and rotating benchmarks. Limits: overlap filters miss paraphrases, and decontamination can itself bias results.

Contamination is not always cheating; web-scale scraping makes it nearly unavoidable. It differs from adaptive overfitting to a public leaderboard through repeated submissions, and from classical leakage such as preprocessing on the full dataset.
terms.Best-of-N jailbreaking:
Best-of-N (BoN) jailbreaking (Hughes et al. 2024) is a black-box attack that repeatedly applies random augmentations to a harmful request, queries the target, and stops when a grader judges a response harmful, up to N samples. Text augmentations include random capitalization and scrambled characters; vision and audio use changes of font, colour, pitch or noise. Each trial is roughly an independent draw with success probability p_i, so success after N tries is 1 - product of (1 - p_i), which rises with N even when each p_i is tiny.

The authors report that attack success rate follows a power-law-like trend in N, letting an attacker extrapolate the samples needed, and report high success against several frontier models at N around ten thousand. Defences include output classifiers, rate limiting, detection of near-duplicate prompts and input normalization.

BoN is not a clever prompt; it exploits non-determinism and fragility. It differs from gradient-based suffix attacks such as GCG (white-box), and from best-of-N sampling with a reward model, which shares the name but improves answers.
terms.Bias-variance tradeoff:
For squared-error regression with y = f(x) + e, E[e] = 0 and Var(e) = s^2, the expected error of a learned predictor f_hat at a point x, taken over training sets and noise, decomposes as Bias^2 + Variance + s^2. Here Bias = E[f_hat(x)] - f(x), Variance = E[(f_hat(x) - E[f_hat(x)])^2], and s^2 is irreducible noise. Low-capacity models tend toward high bias and low variance (underfitting); high-capacity models toward the opposite (overfitting).

The trade-off is managed through model complexity, regularization strength (L2 shrinks variance at the cost of bias), early stopping, ensembling (bagging reduces variance by averaging; boosting reduces bias), more data (reduces variance, not bias) and cross-validation. The classic U-shaped test-error curve is complicated by double descent (Belkin et al. 2019): beyond the interpolation threshold, where models fit the training data exactly, test error can fall again as parameters grow, so heavily overparameterized networks generalize despite low bias and apparently high variance.

'Bias' here is statistical, the systematic error of an estimator, not social bias in data or the additive bias parameter in a layer.
terms.Big O notation:
Big-O notation bounds growth rates. f(n) = O(g(n)) means there exist constants c > 0 and n0 such that f(n) <= c * g(n) for all n >= n0. Omega gives a lower bound and Theta both, a tight bound. For algorithms, f(n) counts basic operations (time) or memory words (space) as a function of input size n, usually worst case. Constants and lower-order terms are dropped, so 3n^2 + 10n + 7 = Theta(n^2).

Common classes in increasing growth: O(1), O(log n) (binary search), O(n) (a scan), O(n log n) (comparison sorting, which has an Omega(n log n) lower bound), O(n^2), O(2^n), O(n!). Caveats: constants matter on small inputs, and hash-table O(1) is expected, not worst-case. Input size must be defined carefully: for numbers, n is the bit length, so trial division up to the square root of m is exponential in the input length.

Big-O is an upper bound, not 'the running time': calling a linear algorithm O(n^2) is true but unhelpful, so Theta is usually what people mean.
terms.Binary search:
Binary search finds a target in a sorted array a[0..n-1] by maintaining an interval [lo, hi] that contains the target if it exists, comparing a[mid] with the target and discarding the half that cannot contain it. Each step halves the interval, so it needs at most floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons: O(log n) time and O(1) space iteratively. It needs random access and a total order matching the sort order.

Compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, not (lo + hi) / 2, which can overflow fixed-width integers. Pick a loop invariant and keep to it: with half-open [lo, hi), loop while lo < hi and set hi = mid or lo = mid + 1. The general form is binary search on the answer: for a monotone predicate P(x) (false...false true...true), find the first x where P holds, which solves minimization problems such as minimum capacity or speed when P can be checked in O(f), for total O(f log range).

It requires monotonic structure, not merely a sorted array, and breaks if the comparison is inconsistent (floating-point noise, a non-transitive comparator).
terms.Binary search tree:
A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree in which every node's key is greater than all keys in its left subtree and less than all keys in its right subtree. In-order traversal therefore visits keys in sorted order. Search, insert and delete follow one root-to-leaf path, costing O(h) for height h. With n nodes, h ranges from floor(log2 n) when balanced to n - 1 for a chain, which a naive BST produces when keys arrive sorted.

Deletion has three cases: a leaf is removed; a node with one child is replaced by that child; a node with two children takes the key of its in-order successor (the minimum of its right subtree), which is then deleted from its old position. Self-balancing trees keep h = O(log n) in the worst case through rotations: AVL trees keep subtree heights within 1 of each other (faster lookups), red-black trees use colour invariants (fewer rotations per update, common in standard-library ordered maps).

A BST is not a heap: a heap orders only parent against children and gives O(1) minimum but no ordered search.
terms.Binary tree:
A binary tree is a rooted tree in which each node has at most two children, distinguished as left and right, so a node with only a left child differs from one with only a right child. A tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges, and its height h (edges on the longest root-to-leaf path) satisfies floor(log2 n) <= h <= n - 1. A perfect tree of height h has 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes; a complete tree fills levels left to right, which allows array storage where node i has children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 (0-indexed), as in binary heaps.

Traversals visit each node once, in O(n) time: depth-first orders (pre-order: node, left, right; in-order: left, node, right; post-order: left, right, node), done recursively or with an explicit stack, and level-order (breadth-first) using a queue. Recursion depth equals the height, so a skewed tree of 10^5 nodes can overflow the call stack; use iteration, or Morris traversal for O(1) extra space.

A binary tree is only a shape and carries no ordering unless it is also a BST or heap.
terms.Bit manipulation:
Bit manipulation applies bitwise operators to the binary representation of integers: AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~) and shifts (<<, >>). Core identities: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative and associative. In two's complement, x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit and x & -x isolates it.

These identities give compact solutions: counting set bits with repeated x &= x - 1 (Kernighan's method, O(popcount)); testing a power of two with x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0; finding the unique element when all others appear twice by XOR-ing everything; enumerating subsets of an n-element set as masks 0 to 2^n - 1, the basis of bitmask dynamic programming. Pitfalls: shifting by the word width or more is undefined in C and C++, and in C, == binds tighter than &.

Bit tricks rarely buy speed on modern compilers, which already turn multiplication and division by powers of two into shifts; their value is compact state and neat algorithms. XOR is addition without carry, exactly addition over the two-element field GF(2).
terms.Black-box analysis:
Black-box analysis treats a model as a function accessible only through queries: the analyst sees inputs and outputs, sometimes with sampled text and, in some APIs, log-probabilities, but not weights, activations or gradients. Techniques include behavioural test suites, red-teaming, counterfactual probing (vary one input element and observe the change), self-report (answers may be unreliable), prefill attacks that force the start of a response, and sampling at scale to estimate rare-event rates.

Limits: it only reveals behaviours you think to elicit; rare or trigger-conditioned behaviours such as backdoors may never appear; a model aware it is being tested may behave differently; and outputs can be unfaithful, for example chain-of-thought that does not reflect the actual computation. To show a failure probability below p with confidence 1 - d after observing no failures takes roughly ln(1/d) / p independent samples.

'Black-box' describes access, not how understandable a model is: a model whose weights you hold is still hard to understand but is not black-box in access. White-box methods (probes, patching, sparse autoencoders) use internals; black-box shows what happens, white-box helps explain why.
